When can I ask OrientDig for a detailed photo?
OrientDig lists detailed-photo requests at product ordering and after warehouse intake. Choose the item and specify the exact view needed, then check the service offered for that order.
Which service shows my parcel before dispatch?
OrientDig lists parcel photography separately from item photography. Choose a parcel view to inspect packing. Choose a detailed item photo when the question concerns a seam, label or measurement.
What should a chest measurement request say?
Name the item and option. Ask for the jacket closed, laid flat and measured from one underarm seam to the other, with both tape endpoints in the frame. Include the required unit.
How can I check whether a shirt has a curved hem?
Ask for the full front and side laid flat with the hem visible. A close crop can hide the difference between front and back length. Compare against the construction shown for the selected option.
How do I request the most useful picture of a fragile item?
Specify the component and the possible problem, such as the handle joint or a chipped rim. Ask for enough of the whole piece to identify it and a close view that resolves the concern.
Should I request a parcel photo to measure an individual shoe?
A parcel view documents packing. Ask for an item-level photo showing the specified shoe and measurement endpoints if your decision depends on fit.
What does rehearsal packing help me check?

OrientDig describes packing the selected items to obtain a parcel weight before submission. Keep the selected contents and packing instructions with the result, especially if you may change the parcel later.
Which result becomes stale if I add another item after rehearsal?
The prior packed weight applies to the earlier contents. Recheck dimensions, weight and available routes for the revised parcel before relying on the earlier comparison.
How can I verify both pieces of a matching set?
Give the warehouse the selected seller option and name each included piece. Request a single overview showing both together before requesting detail photos of a particular piece.
What information helps identify two nearly identical orders?
Give the order references and each exact size or colour. Ask for separate views with the identifying label visible so that measurements do not get assigned to the wrong garment.
What if I cannot see the start of the tape in a detailed photo?
Explain which endpoint is missing and request a full measurement view. A number at the far end is insufficient when the start may be folded, offset or outside the frame.
When should I look into a storage extension?
Check the intake date and deadline of each individual item. OrientDig's service page gives eligibility conditions for extensions. Confirm the item qualifies before waiting for a different order.
How do I compare packing around two fragile components?
Describe which surfaces must not touch and which accessories should remain separate. Ask for a view before sealing if the arrangement affects your decision to dispatch.
Can I compare seller measurements given from different starting points?
First repeat both methods on a garment you own. For example, back length from the collar seam differs from length measured from the high shoulder point, even on the same jacket.
What should I save when the warehouse confirms a request?
Save the item reference, your request and the returned image or result together. A parcel weight in a message can be hard to interpret later unless its list of contents is recorded.
Which page lists prices for extra pictures and packing services?
Open OrientDig's Value Added Services page, then check the service and charge offered in your account. Distinguish charges per item, photograph and parcel when assembling a budget.
How can I keep the original retail box without confusing it with the outer carton?

Identify the product box by the item and warehouse reference. State whether the branded box should remain with the item, then describe the separate protective shipping carton. Ask the warehouse to confirm the instruction before repacking.
Can I use a laid-flat chest reading as a circumference?

The photograph records the distance between the two endpoints shown. Doubling a straight pit-to-pit reading gives an approximate circumference for comparison, provided the garment lies flat and you compare it with a garment measured the same way.
Which tracking update confirms a local carrier has received my parcel?

Look for an acceptance or physical scan by the named carrier. An electronic notification can appear before that handoff. Save the tracking numbers for both legs so you can compare the two carrier histories.
What details belong in a shopping assistant request for a multicolour listing?

Provide the seller URL, exact option text, requested quantity and the colour shown in the selected variant. State whether substitutions are acceptable. A picture of the whole listing can show colours that are unavailable in your size.
What should I compare when a logistics route disappears after repacking?

Compare the destination, declared contents, packed length, width, height and weight before and after the change. Check the selected route’s published conditions and ask support about the specific changed field if the estimator gives no explanation.
How to request an OrientDig detailed photo that answers your QC question
An extra warehouse picture is worth requesting when it changes a decision. Pick the feature, angle and scale before you send the request, then check whether the returned image actually shows them.
Decide what would make you accept or question the item

Suppose a jacket has reached the OrientDig warehouse. The standard pictures show its front and back, but you ordered it for a particular reason: the two-way front zip should open from the bottom when you sit down. You can see a silver pull near the collar. You cannot see what is attached at the hem. Asking for “better QC” gives the photographer little direction. Asking for a front photograph of the fully closed zip, with the lower end and both sliders in focus, turns the same uncertainty into a job somebody can complete.

OrientDig's detailed photo page distinguishes the usual warehouse views from pictures taken to a customer's specification. It asks buyers to identify a stored item by number and match the number of purchased photographs to their requirements. Use that distinction before spending time on a request. If an existing picture is simply blurred, read the page's guidance on retakes. If the existing photo is clear but shows the wrong angle for your question, a custom detail request may be appropriate. Check the available option and price on the specific order.
Identify the physical unit before describing the shot

The seller's marketplace item number can describe a listing containing several colours and sizes. The warehouse reference identifies the unit being handled. Give both when they serve different purposes. If two jackets from the same listing have arrived, say which warehouse entry you want photographed and which selection you expect it to contain. For example, “warehouse item [number], short navy jacket, size L” is a much better starting point than a screenshot of the listing with no reference. Replace the placeholder with your actual record inside the private order channel.

Look over your original selection before telling the warehouse what you expect to find. A seller's model picture might show the jacket with a belt even though one option is sold without it. Asking the photographer to confirm that a belt is missing already assumes the answer. A more useful request is “please show the jacket and all included detachable pieces laid out together.” Save the paid option wording beside the returned picture. You can then decide whether the visible contents match the purchase, independently of what appeared on the listing's first image.
Specify the angle and the feature in ordinary language

Describe what should remain inside the frame. For a zip, that might be both ends of the fastening in one front view. For a printed number, ask for the entire print and enough of the surrounding panel to show placement. For a bag clasp, ask for the open clasp and the point where it attaches. Instructions like “best angle” leave the photographer to guess which aspect matters. Use a short sentence naming the side, part and desired state: open or closed, flat or upright, with or without an attached accessory.

Consider scale. A close crop can show a chipped button but leave you unable to tell which button it is. A whole-garment image can identify the button but compress the chip into a few pixels. If both questions affect the decision, request two clearly different views. In the first, identify the button's location relative to a pocket or seam. In the second, show the surface in focus. OrientDig's guidance links the requested content to the photo quantity. Check whether the views you describe fit the service you select.
Give a measurement two endpoints and a unit

A tape measure sitting on a garment is not automatically evidence of the dimension you need. Decide where the measurement should begin and end. For a flat chest width, that usually means naming the underarm seams on a garment laid flat with the front closed. Ask for both ends of the tape and its reading in the same photograph. Explain if the item should be relaxed rather than stretched. The important point is consistency with the garment or diagram you are using as your comparison.

A request for “jacket length” is especially easy to misinterpret. The centre back from the collar seam to the hem can produce a different figure from a measurement starting at the high shoulder point. A collar included in one measurement and excluded in another changes it again. If your reference chart uses a diagram, point to its specific path in your note. Write the unit. A precise request could say “please measure in centimetres from the centre back collar seam, excluding the collar itself, straight to the bottom hem, with the entire tape visible.”
Use a reference image to clarify rather than prove

A seller image or another buyer's picture can help you indicate the detail you mean. Explain its role: “this image shows which seam I mean,” or “the two arrows mark the endpoints I use.” Do not assume that the reference photograph shows the same batch, version or size as your order. The photograph you need for your decision is the one of your actual warehouse item. Keep the original source and the returned photographs separate in your notes so their origins remain clear after several orders.

For a colour question, a reference can be less conclusive than it appears. A phone display, studio lighting and warehouse lighting can all make dark navy look black. Ask for the colour or option label and, if offered, a wider picture under neutral lighting with another identifiable object in view. The label can support the identity of the purchased option. The picture can help you judge appearance. Neither can guarantee the exact shade you will perceive outdoors. Decide whether the remaining uncertainty matters enough to delay a parcel.
Review the result against the request line by line

Open the returned picture next to your note. Can you recognize the relevant unit? Is the requested part visible? Is the image sharp at the place where you need detail? If a measurement is involved, can you follow the tape continuously from the chosen start to the end and read the unit? If the answers are yes, record the observation rather than a general impression. For the jacket that might read “both sliders visible on the short navy unit.” That note gives a clear reason to proceed even if you later view the pictures out of order.

If the result misses something important, identify exactly what is unresolved. “The photograph shows the top slider, but the lower ten centimetres of the zip are outside the frame” gives a photographer a concrete correction. A cropped tape reading without its starting point is a different problem from a tape that follows the wrong seam. OrientDig's detailed photo instructions discuss requesting another view when requirements have not been met. Refer to the original instruction and the actual image when raising the issue, and check the service conditions shown for your order.
Stop when you have enough evidence for the decision

More images can be distracting when they revisit a question already settled. Once you know which version arrived, which visible feature it has and how its measured dimensions compare with yours, write down the outstanding issue, if any. A photo cannot establish long-term durability or show how an item feels after wearing it for a day. Separate those uncertainties from questions a warehouse photographer can realistically resolve. That keeps a request proportionate to the decision you need to make before shipment.

Finally, keep the item pictures tied to their warehouse reference when preparing your parcel. OrientDig lists parcel photography separately from detailed item photography. A photograph of the packed parcel can be valuable for checking the arrangement of several pieces, but by that stage the zip or measurement may no longer be accessible. Resolve the item-level decision while the individual unit can still be inspected, then use any parcel-level service for the distinct question it is designed to answer.

How to measure a garment from OrientDig warehouse photos
Two tape readings can disagree even when both are accurate. Use the seller's diagram and a garment you own to specify the path, endpoints and units of each warehouse measurement.
Choose a comparison garment with a similar shape

A tape-measure photo becomes useful when you have something meaningful to compare it with. Choose a garment you already wear in the way you intend to wear the new piece. A fitted shirt worn alone gives a poor reference for a jacket intended to fit over a sweatshirt. Button or zip the reference as you normally would. Lay it on a flat surface, smooth major folds and avoid pulling stretchy fabric tight. Record how you positioned it. Repeating that setup is more valuable than trying to measure every dimension on the garment.

Start with the question that matters for your purchase. If sleeves routinely come up short, concentrate on sleeve construction and cuff position. If a jacket must fit a particular layer underneath, concentrate on chest width with the front closed. If you care where the hem sits, define length carefully. OrientDig describes detailed photos as a way to request views of specific features and measurements. One carefully chosen measurement can resolve a buying decision better than several numbers taken by methods you cannot identify.
Read the seller's diagram before naming a dimension

Look for arrows or illustrations that show the start and finish of the measurement. A chart can report body measurements, finished garment measurements or a set of recommended sizes. A chest figure on a body chart can include intended ease in the garment design. A tape photographed across a flat garment measures the object itself. Even if the figures use the same unit, they do not necessarily describe the same thing. Keep the chart's heading and diagram in your reference note as well as the row of numbers.

Consider a hypothetical chart with a chest figure of 110 centimetres. If it describes the full circumference of a finished, symmetrical garment laid flat, a width near 55 centimetres may be consistent. If it describes the body for which the garment was designed, simply halving the value does not tell you the finished width. Pleats, layering, thickness and style can all change the relationship. When the chart is ambiguous, request an observable flat width and compare it directly with your own reference. Avoid treating an inferred conversion as a confirmed specification.
Request chest width in one continuous view

For a jacket with ordinary set-in sleeves, describe the measurement from the junction of one underarm seam to the junction of the other. Ask for the front closed, the garment flat and the tape straight without tension. If the armholes are unusually deep or the garment has a batwing shape, the conventional endpoints may be hard to locate. In that case, choose a reproducible point on the garment or ask for an overview first. Explain where you measured your own piece so the warehouse can decide whether the requested method is practical.

Review the resulting photo in three stages. First identify the correct warehouse item and marked size. Next trace the path of the tape across the garment. Finally inspect the zero mark and reading at the far end. A clear number on the right tells you little if the tape started several centimetres beyond the left seam. If one edge is outside the frame, state which one when requesting clarification. “Please include the left underarm and the zero mark” is easier to resolve than “the measurement looks wrong.”
Distinguish centre-back length from high-shoulder length

Place your reference garment face down. For a centre-back measurement, decide whether to begin at the seam where the collar joins the back or at the top of the collar itself. Follow the centre line to the hem. For a high-shoulder measurement, begin at the high shoulder point near the neck and follow the specified path to the hem. On a garment with a shaped neckline or curved hem, these paths can produce different numbers. Write down which hem point matters if the sides and centre differ.

Suppose your reference measures 62 centimetres from the back collar seam while the seller lists 66 centimetres from the high shoulder point. These hypothetical numbers do not demonstrate a four-centimetre error. Before making a decision, measure your reference by both methods or request the seller's path on the new piece. If you particularly need to know how far a jacket reaches in the back, prioritize the centre-back result even if the seller's chart uses the shoulder. The purpose is a usable comparison, not forcing two unlike measurements to match.
Match sleeve measurements to the construction

Set-in sleeves have a recognizable shoulder seam. A request from shoulder seam to cuff can work when the shoulder falls in roughly the same place on both garments. Dropped shoulders move that seam down the arm, shortening the apparent sleeve segment despite a similar overall reach. Raglan sleeves start at the neckline and have no conventional shoulder endpoint. Check the construction in the standard photograph before deciding how to describe the path. Comparing a dropped-shoulder sleeve length with a fitted shirt sleeve can produce a misleading impression of fit.

One practical alternative is a neck-to-cuff measurement. Specify the neck point, whether the tape should follow the top edge or another path and whether the cuff should lie flat. Measure the comparable path on your own garment. If the sleeve is designed to curve, decide whether to follow the seam or draw a straight line; the two methods answer different questions. In your request, ask for the full route in one frame if readable, or an overview plus a second close view of the reading if that fits the available photo service.
Evaluate elastic, cuffs and layered construction

An elastic waistband has more than one meaningful width. A relaxed flat width describes it at rest. A stretched measurement depends on the force applied and can be hard to reproduce. Decide which information is necessary and avoid requesting an extreme stretch that might damage an item. For a ribbed cuff, measure the opening the same way on your own garment. A doubled flat width is only an approximation of circumference for a thick or irregular opening. Label it accordingly in your notes.

A lined coat can have a generous outer width while the interior or sleeve opening limits movement. A photo cannot fully recreate how it feels over the clothing you plan to wear. Identify which measurements can reduce uncertainty and which questions remain about fabric, movement or comfort. If the decisive question is whether a cuff accommodates a particular glove, ask for the relevant opening measurement rather than a general front width. Keep the result tied to the exact option because other versions within the same listing may have different construction.
Make a decision the evidence can support

Write one short line for each dimension you actually used. Include the item, size, date, endpoints, unit and observed result. Put the comparable measurement from your own garment beside it. Where the two methods disagree, mark the comparison unresolved rather than recording a difference as a defect. This becomes particularly useful when you have similar items from several sellers: the note tells you which tape photo belongs to which decision without relying on the order in a gallery.

If a result appears to conflict with the seller's stated measurement, keep the chart and photo together and ask a precise question before dispatch. Point out the relevant size row and the endpoints visible in the returned picture. A difference in method may explain it. If the method matches and the difference affects your decision, use the order's current support process while the item can still be inspected. Your final decision should describe what you learned about this garment, with its own construction and measurements, rather than making a general claim about how a labelled size will fit every buyer.

Planning an OrientDig parcel around a fragile find

A photograph of an intact item and a photograph of its packing answer different questions. Decide what needs protection, which evidence to request and which route conditions still require confirmation.
Start with the part most likely to suffer damage

Take an ordinary ceramic cup with a curved handle. The main body can look substantial while the handle projects beyond it and joins at two narrow points. A product photograph taken from the front may show a perfect printed design and hide one of those joints. If the reason you would reject the cup is a cracked handle, your first question belongs to the individual warehouse item. Ask for a clear view of the handle and its attachment points while the cup is accessible. Save that view beside the purchase option and item reference.

Make a short list of the parts whose condition matters. On a presentation box it could be the corners and closure. On a framed piece it could be the glass edge and surface. On the cup, add the rim and base if a chip would affect your use. The list should drive a small number of useful inspections. A large gallery of decorative details can still miss the vulnerable part. OrientDig lists detailed item photography and parcel photography separately. Choose the former to examine the item itself and the latter to document how the parcel is prepared.
Decide what role the seller's packaging plays

Before authorizing disposal of any original packing, ask what the components do. A fitted insert might keep the cup from moving, while a decorative sleeve merely improves presentation. A retail carton might be part of a gift you intend to give. Another carton might be damaged already or unsuitable for the next journey. Photograph the item and existing packaging together, then decide whether you need protection, presentation, a record for an after-sales inquiry or all three. Removing a piece is much easier than restoring it.

A request to “remove all boxes and pack safely” can contain conflicting intentions. If the fitted insert is the only feature that supports a fragile handle, stripping it out solely to reduce volume may work against your priority. Describe the functional requirement instead. For example: “Please confirm whether the cup can remain supported in its fitted insert and whether the outer retail sleeve can be omitted without exposing the handle.” Ask about available services and any return implications before authorizing the change. The warehouse can respond more usefully to a concrete arrangement than a general request for maximum safety.
Check how the fragile piece interacts with the other contents

A cup travelling with a sweatshirt poses a different packing question from a cup travelling with metal hardware. Soft clothing in the same parcel is not automatically adequate cushioning. A hard object can move or press against a protruding part if it is positioned carelessly. Write down the exact warehouse entries intended for the parcel and identify any surfaces that should remain separate. If a heavy accessory can move, say so before the parcel is sealed. Avoid specifying a construction you cannot assess; explain the risks you want the packer to address.

Compare the combined shipment with a separate parcel for the fragile piece. Separation can simplify protection, but another parcel may carry its own minimum charges and packing costs. The combined parcel may be larger or have fewer eligible routes. Price and protection are different columns in this decision. Compare eligible options for the same destination and real contents. Check carrier and platform conditions for that type of item. A route appearing for general merchandise does not settle whether a particular fragile object is accepted or covered for breakage.
Ask for evidence at the point when it can still help

OrientDig's service list describes photographs before and after sealing for its parcel-photo service. A pre-seal image can help show where the cup sits relative to a heavy accessory and whether the original insert appears to be present. A sealed-box image can help identify the outside condition or parcel markings. Neither image can prove what happened between carrier handoffs, nor can it establish every hidden layer of protective material. Decide what you expect to see in the open view before choosing the service.

A useful note might read: “For parcel [reference], the cup is warehouse item [number]. If the available service allows, show that the handle is supported and that the metal accessory is in a separate area before sealing.” If your question needs a close item-level inspection, resolve it earlier. A wide photograph of four packed pieces will seldom make a fine crack visible. If the returned image cannot resolve the concern, identify the missing view without assuming that the absence of visible cushioning means no cushioning exists behind the item.
Account for the space that protection requires

Protective packing can change a box's external dimensions more than it changes its actual weight. Measure or obtain all three external dimensions and the packed mass for the arrangement you intend to use. OrientDig describes rehearsal packing as a way to obtain a parcel weight before submission. Confirm which measurements are available for your parcel and whether later changes require a revised estimate. Keep the list of included items with the measurement record. A result for a cup and two shirts cannot conclusively price a later parcel that also contains a large box.

Imagine a hypothetical retail carton measuring 18 by 15 by 14 centimetres. An outer shipment box needs to be larger if space is used to protect the original carton. Entering the retail dimensions into a route comparison would understate that scenario. There is no need to invent a standard allowance for every parcel. Mark the figure as unknown until you have a plausible outer size, and test several clearly labelled possibilities if you need an early budget. Use the actual billing rules shown for each route rather than assuming a single volume formula applies everywhere.
Read the service conditions in terms of your particular object

Before paying, check whether the selected service lists restrictions for fragile contents, requirements about original packaging or exclusions for particular damage. Record the current wording beside the route name and date. A general statement that a parcel service offers protection does not identify what evidence is needed or whether a specific chip is covered. Ask the platform a narrow question when the written conditions leave a decisive point unresolved. Include the item material and packing proposal so the response addresses the right case.

If you decide to send the parcel, keep the seller description, warehouse item photo, packing instructions and parcel reference in one place. Record what the photographs actually show. “Handle and both joints visible before packing” is stronger documentation than “item checked.” “Outer box visibly closed” describes the post-seal photo accurately. Avoid writing “unbreakable packing” or “fully insured” unless a specific service statement really supports that conclusion. A clear record is useful whether the item arrives intact or there is an issue to investigate.
Examine the delivered parcel before discarding its packaging

At delivery, identify the correct parcel by its label and check the exterior for signs relevant to the item. If you discover damage, keep the packaging, inserts and affected pieces. Photograph the outer carton, arrangement and precise damaged area. Use the parcel reference for the delivery and the warehouse item reference for the cup. Look at the current reporting process promptly. Dates, evidence requirements and available remedies depend on the applicable terms, so a screenshot from a previous order should not be your sole guide.

When the parcel arrives intact, the same records still have value. Compare the actual packing with your instructions and the amount you paid. Identify which features were useful and which created bulk without answering a need. Next time you can describe the exact protective function you want, ask for the right photograph at the right stage and compare quotes using more realistic dimensions. That specific knowledge is more useful than a general rating of an entire shipping route based on a single parcel.

Matching an OrientDig warehouse arrival to the right seller order

One seller can split a purchase into two domestic shipments, and one delivery can contain several variants. Reconcile the original order, carrier record and warehouse entry before deciding a piece is missing.
Give the purchase a unit list before tracking starts

Imagine a purchase containing a cap and two belts, one brown and one black. The seller calls the whole thing “accessories” and the confirmation fits on one screen. You will have a much easier time checking arrival if you write down three physical units before the first parcel is shipped. Include the seller name, original listing, selected option text and quantity for each. If a belt includes a detachable buckle or comes as a gift set, record what the purchased option actually includes. The seller's display photo can show pieces sold separately.

OrientDig's shopping-assistant guide begins with the original product link or a search result from which the buyer selects an item. Preserve that selection when moving from shopping to tracking. A warehouse photo may identify an object as a belt but still leave open whether it is the narrow or wide version from your order. A seller option label, a model code or a stated width gives you something specific to match. Without it, a later disagreement becomes an argument about whether two similar photographs look alike.
Separate the marketplace identifier from both tracking numbers

A marketplace product identifier identifies a listing. A domestic courier number identifies a particular trip to the warehouse. An international tracking number, if you later submit a parcel, concerns a different journey. Give each field its own label. If you paste all three into a note under “order number,” the longest string can easily be mistaken for the number a support form is requesting. Also retain the OrientDig purchase or warehouse reference displayed for the item. The platform uses its own records to locate what it is handling.

Look at the destination as well as the event. If a domestic carrier says the package was delivered to a location in China, the event may concern seller delivery to the warehouse. It is not evidence that a parcel has reached your overseas address. OrientDig describes its international logistics chain separately, beginning with warehouse packing and collection by a logistics provider. Unless you have submitted an outbound shipment and can identify its parcel record, do not jump from a domestic delivery scan to an international delivery conclusion.
Map one seller to several domestic shipments

Suppose the cap is dispatched on Monday and the two belts on Wednesday. Record each tracking number with the items the seller says it covers, if that information is available. Mark the assignment as reported rather than physically verified until the warehouse evidence appears. When the first shipment is delivered, the outstanding list should still contain the belts. If the seller provides no contents breakdown, enter both tracking numbers against the purchase and wait to assign units until you have better evidence.

A single delivery can also cover items shown on different purchase lines. A seller may pack both belts together, while the warehouse later creates separate item references for the colours. That difference in grouping is not an error by itself. Count physical units and map them across the stages. One domestic parcel, two belts and two warehouse entries can describe the same transaction accurately. Conversely, two warehouse images do not prove that there are two belts; they could show both sides of one belt. Ask which object a count describes before treating the numbers as inconsistent.
Check the strongest identifying details first

At intake, read the available labels and order-specific markings. For the belts, compare buckle shape, strap width and selected colour. For the cap, compare size or fastening type if these differ across the listing. A large photo of a plain black accessory might be visually correct but not distinctive enough to assign to one of two similar sellers. A visible model code, option label or unusual feature carries more identifying information. Keep that evidence attached to the warehouse reference rather than just saving a picture named “black.”

When the existing view leaves an important detail unclear, consider what additional observation would resolve it. OrientDig's detailed-photo instructions ask for the stored item's number and allow the buyer to specify a view. A useful request might ask for both belt buckles and a close view of the width label on the brown one. If you need a measurement, state the endpoints and unit. A general request to photograph “everything again” may produce a clearer image of the same uninformative surface while leaving the identity unresolved.
Distinguish three kinds of missing-item question

First, a piece may still be on the seller side. Check the purchase status and any domestic tracking information before asking the warehouse to search for something that has not been dispatched. Second, a domestic shipment may have a delivery scan but no warehouse record you can match. In that case, supply the seller tracking reference, destination information and expected contents to the order channel. Third, a warehouse entry may exist but its visible contents may conflict with the order. Give the item reference and identify exactly which expected piece or variation is absent.

For example, “missing brown belt” could mean the seller shipped only the cap, two belts arrived in one packet but only the black one is visible, or you found two black belts despite ordering different colours. Each case calls for a different next check. A short support message should contain the last confirmed stage and the first unresolved one. “Domestic carrier marks package [reference] delivered; warehouse entry [reference] shows the black belt; I expected the brown belt in that same shipment” gives a clearer starting point than “my order did not arrive.”
Reconcile a corrected or exchanged unit without losing the history

If a seller later sends a replacement, add it as a new shipment linked to the original purchase. Do not overwrite the old tracking number with the new one. Retain the reason for the replacement and the promised option. Otherwise, when two warehouse entries appear over time, it may look as if you bought two units intentionally. Mark whether the original item is awaiting return, held for inspection or otherwise accounted for according to your actual order record.

When the replacement arrives, repeat the specific check that motivated the exchange. If the issue was width, examine the width or measurement on the replacement. If it was the colour code, look for that code and the selected order text. An improved photograph of an unrelated feature cannot establish that the earlier issue was corrected. Record the result against the replacement reference, not the original. This separation becomes essential if the two units are present in the warehouse during overlapping periods and you later choose one for shipment.
Submit the international parcel from the reconciled list

Before you send anything overseas, mark each intended unit as matched, disputed or still expected. Select warehouse references for the matched pieces and compare their count with the outbound list. If you knowingly ship the cap now and wait for the belts, record that choice. A later difference between purchase count and parcel count can then be explained immediately. Check dates and storage conditions for pieces held behind; a deliberate hold still needs a review date.

Once the outbound record exists, associate its reference with those selected units. Use its tracking information for the journey overseas. Keep the domestic references for questions about seller shipment or warehouse intake. If the parcel arrives and something is missing, compare the contents first with the outbound selection, then with the purchase history. That order of comparison prevents a piece left in storage from being described as lost in international transit, while preserving the evidence needed if a confirmed selected unit genuinely cannot be accounted for.

Checking an OrientDig two-piece set before sending it overseas
A model wearing a complete outfit does not identify the option you paid for. Verify set contents, component sizes and shared details while the individual pieces are still at the warehouse.
Read the selected offer one piece at a time

Imagine you are buying a matching overshirt and shorts. The first seller photograph shows the two together; the option list offers shirt, shorts and a set. Before looking at the warehouse images, find the actual selected option on your purchase record. Save its original wording, quantity and size. An order for one shirt and one pair of shorts on separate purchase lines is different from an order for one set sold as a single unit. Both can produce two garments, but the seller's obligations and available exchange options may differ.

Now check whether any additional accessory is part of the selected offer. A belt visible on the model may be included, removable but sold separately, or part of the styling. If the listing is ambiguous, ask a specific question before paying or authorizing shipment. “Does the selected navy set include the belt shown in image three?” is precise. “Is everything included?” leaves the answer dependent on what each person understands by everything. Keep the seller or agent response beside the option rather than relying on the original marketing picture alone.
Match the ordered size combination to the set

Some listings present one size for the entire set, while others let the buyer select top and bottom independently. Read the actual selectors. If you need medium on top and large on the bottom, a quantity field cannot communicate that combination by itself. Do not assume a note can override the way the seller stocks a prepacked set. Ask whether a mixed-size combination is available and obtain confirmation if it is essential. Retain the source selection and any agreed changes within the purchase record.

Define the measurements that matter for each piece. A shirt's flat chest width and back length describe different questions from the shorts' relaxed waistband width and rise. A single “fits medium” statement is too vague to compare the outfit. Choose a comparable top and bottom that you own and record the same endpoints as the seller's diagrams. If your decision depends more on the bottom than the top, prioritize that detail in any warehouse photo request rather than asking for a large collection of general pictures.
Establish that the parts belong together

When warehouse pictures become available, begin with an overview showing all pieces laid out together if available. It helps count the garments and see whether one is obviously a different colour or pattern. Compare labels, model codes and distinguishing features where possible. The same shade name can apply to several versions. A navy overshirt with a fine stripe and plain navy shorts may be intentional or may indicate two unrelated pieces, depending on the purchased option. Check the seller description before declaring a mismatch.

Be careful with camera exposure. Two separately photographed dark garments can appear different under changing light. A single shot under common lighting gives a more useful comparison, especially if colour coordination is central to the set. Look at texture and pattern spacing as well as apparent shade. A photograph can reveal a visible difference; it cannot fully establish how fabrics will look outdoors or after washing. Record what the picture actually shows, for example “both pieces in one frame, same visible stripe spacing,” instead of making a promise about identical fabric composition.
Request the one missing piece of evidence

OrientDig's detailed-photo guidance allows instructions about a particular angle, feature or measurement. Give the stored item's reference and state what you need to decide. If the overview shows both garments but no size labels, ask for a view identifying each label and the corresponding piece. If the seller promised a detachable belt, ask for both pieces and the belt laid out together. If the top has a distinctive embroidered cuff, request that cuff specifically. Choose a number of views consistent with the service you select.

For example, a two-view request might ask for the whole set with the visible accessories, followed by an image of the shorts' waistband tape measurement. That gives one count check and one fit check. If you also need a readable top label, consider whether it can be shown clearly in the first frame or needs its own view. Avoid packing several incompatible requests into one close-up. A photograph wide enough to show an entire outfit will often make a small printed label unreadable on a phone.
Evaluate fit without mixing body and garment figures

For the top, close buttons or zips if that matches the seller's measurement method. Ask for a straight flat width at named seams or a named length path. For the shorts, distinguish relaxed elastic width from a measurement under tension. A stretched elastic result depends on the force applied and can be difficult to reproduce. Measure your own garment with the same method. Compare the two observations rather than assuming an identical size label means identical dimensions across different sellers or styles.

Consider a hypothetical case in which your reference shorts measure 36 centimetres across the relaxed waistband and the warehouse photo seems to show 72 centimetres. Before deciding there is an enormous difference, verify whether one number refers to the full circumference. Also inspect where the tape begins and whether the garment is stretched. A chart may quote recommended body circumference instead of finished garment circumference. Name the measurement type when asking for clarification. Correcting a unit or endpoint misunderstanding can resolve a concern without changing the order.
Handle a partial mismatch as a set-level question

Suppose the shirt is correct and the shorts are the wrong size. Record expected and observed sizes separately. Save the purchase option showing whether the set was sold together and ask the order channel what options apply. Do not assume the seller will exchange the shorts alone or require both pieces back; that depends on the actual terms and item. Keep packaging and tags while the issue is being assessed. If any service could alter return condition, such as removing labels or discarding a presentation box, hold that decision until you understand the consequences.

If a replacement is offered, clarify what will be sent and what must be returned. If only the bottom is replaced, the colour match may need another check when it arrives. Keep the original set reference and replacement reference distinct. Ask for evidence of the specific corrected feature before combining the pieces again. A second photograph showing the correct shorts size does not identify whether the replacement matches the fabric of the retained top, so revisit the questions that originally made the coordinated set worth buying.
Check both pieces at packing and receipt

When the set is ready, look at how its warehouse records are represented in the parcel selection. Two components might appear together under one entry or separately. Match the selected entries with your completed unit list. If you intentionally send the top in one parcel and leave the bottom behind, document that choice. Otherwise, verify that both pieces are accounted for before dispatch. A parcel count of one can be correct for a complete set sold and stored together, but it cannot prove the physical count without context.

At delivery, keep the set together while comparing its contents with your saved overview and options. If a question arises, give both the original purchase reference and the outbound parcel reference. Explain which component is affected and what the earlier warehouse evidence showed. This gives support a meaningful timeline rather than a general complaint about an outfit. When everything matches, retain the measurements alongside the seller information for future sizing decisions. Your own verified comparison of this cut will be much more useful than a general claim that every set from a platform runs large or small.

Which retail packaging should you keep for an OrientDig parcel?
A retail box may protect a product, complete a gift or preserve an unresolved return option. Decide what it does before comparing the cost of keeping or removing it.
Identify the packaging layer you are talking about

An item can arrive inside a protective bag, a fitted insert, a retail box, a seller transport carton and another layer used for outbound international shipping. “Remove the box” is ambiguous when several boxes are involved. Ask which layer the warehouse means and describe it in plain language. For example, “the brown seller delivery carton outside the printed shoebox” identifies a different object from “the printed box holding the shoes.” Preserve photographs of the packaging arrangement when a distinction matters to your decision.

Begin with why you want a change. Perhaps the retail box is empty space around a soft accessory. Perhaps you want it intact because it is part of a present. Perhaps the corner of the box is damaged and you are deciding whether to return the item. Each reason suggests a different course. Do not authorize disposal before settling a return or exchange question. The seller's conditions and the handling already performed can affect the available options. Seek a specific answer for your actual order while the relevant materials still exist.
Separate protection, presentation and evidence

A fitted insert can keep a fragile object away from the sides of a carton. A decorative sleeve may improve presentation while adding little structural protection. A printed label may identify the version or ingredients of an item even if the container itself is thin. Write a short note for each part: protects a projecting piece, holds small accessories together, identifies the purchased version, or matters to the recipient. This gives the warehouse a clearer description of what must be preserved than asking to retain “important packaging.”

Think about who will receive the goods. A replacement item for personal use may be acceptable in plain protective packing. A gift set meant to be handed over as presented may be incomplete without the display carton. If a box is part of the product's value to you, include its condition in your warehouse review. Ask for photographs of the relevant surfaces and corners before the item enters an outbound parcel. A later image of a sealed shipping box will tell you little about a dented presentation carton inside it.
Compare actual mass with the space the box uses

A light box can matter to international freight because of its dimensions. OrientDig's billing-weight guidance describes estimating parcel packing and applying volumetric weight on applicable routes when it exceeds actual weight. Use the route's own terms for any calculation. Dimensions taken from a seller's retail box do not necessarily describe the outer international parcel; additional protection may increase them. Record which object you measured and whether the figures are observed, estimated or supplied after packing.

As an illustration, compare a rectangular box measuring 32 by 22 by 13 centimetres with a flatter arrangement of 32 by 22 by 8. Their external volumes are 9,152 and 5,632 cubic centimetres respectively. That difference of 3,520 cubic centimetres is a change in physical volume. It is not a guaranteed monetary saving. The shipping carton may have different dimensions, another item may already determine its height or the selected route may bill on actual weight. Use the example to identify a question for the estimator, not a discount to subtract from your budget.
Compare scenarios for the entire parcel

Create a keep scenario and a remove scenario with the same contents, destination and relevant route assumptions. In each, identify the outer dimensions you expect and the protection the item would receive. If the shoe box would be placed beside another rigid carton of the same height, discarding it may leave the outer parcel's dimensions unchanged. If it is the longest or tallest piece, the effect could be greater. The packing arrangement matters as much as the volume of the individual box.

If you request rehearsal packing, specify the actual list of items and which packaging layers must remain. OrientDig lists rehearsal packing as an optional way to get a packed parcel weight before submission. Check what figures are returned for your order. Changing the contents, discarding a box afterwards or asking for stronger outer protection can make the earlier result less applicable. Keep the record of which scenario was measured. A number without its contents and instructions is difficult to compare with the final parcel.
Avoid exchanging a known benefit for a speculative saving

A shoebox may protect the shape of the shoes or separate them from other contents. A jewellery box may keep small parts in one place. An electronics package may contain a fitted support tray that holds components apart. Removing these layers might be reasonable, but replacement protection should be considered. Describe which surfaces must remain separated and which small accessories need to travel together. Ask what packing options are actually offered rather than assuming that clothes elsewhere in the parcel will provide sufficient cushioning.

Evaluate the trade in concrete terms. Suppose preserving a box keeps a gift ready to present, while removing it might allow a smaller outer carton. If neither the final dimensions nor the route charge is known, the gift value is established and the freight saving is uncertain. You can investigate the uncertainty with a quote, choose to retain the box, or decide that the box has no value to the recipient. The right choice depends on the purchase. General statements such as “always remove shoe boxes” ignore the reason somebody bought that particular item.
Write instructions that a packer can distinguish

Use the warehouse item reference and name the packaging to keep and remove. One example: “For item [reference], keep the printed gift carton, fitted tray and accessory envelope together. The plain seller courier carton may be omitted if suitable outer protection is available. Please ask if this is unclear.” Adjust the instruction to the choices the service actually allows. A concise positive description of the pieces to retain is safer than a long list of materials that might all be called packaging.

If you need a visual record, distinguish item-level detailed photos from parcel photos. An item photo can document the condition of the printed box before packing. A pre-seal parcel view can help identify its placement relative to other goods. A sealed view can show exterior condition. OrientDig's published value-added services describe these different stages. Check the service description and order screen rather than assuming every photograph is included. Request the view that can still answer your question at that stage.
Record the decision and check the result at delivery

Before submission, save your chosen scenario, the reasons for keeping or removing each layer and any agreed service charge. Confirm the route accepts the actual contents. If your decision relied on keeping material intact for an exchange, verify that the exchange question has genuinely been resolved before authorizing an irreversible packing change. Once the parcel is sent, keep its reference with those instructions. If you need to ask about a discrepancy, cite the particular item and packaging layer rather than describing the whole shipment as incorrectly packed.

At delivery, compare the packaging you received with the instruction and the visible condition documented earlier. If damage is present, retain the outer carton, internal protection and item packaging while you check the reporting procedure. If the trade worked well, save the actual dimensions and final charge for context when planning a similar parcel. That experience can improve your next estimate, but changes in contents, routes and pricing still deserve a fresh comparison. A good packaging decision can be explained in terms of the item it protected and the cost evidence available when you made it.

Comparing OrientDig packed dimensions before you choose a route
A shorter box can matter more than a lighter one, or make no price difference at all. Compare two packing arrangements using the current route rules and the same actual contents.
Name the two arrangements you are comparing

Start with a concrete decision. Perhaps you want to keep the printed retail box around a pair of shoes but are willing to remove an oversized seller carton. Or you have a jacket that can be folded more compactly if doing so will not damage its shape. Give the proposed arrangements short descriptions tied to the actual physical changes. “Shoes in retail box beside folded jacket” and “shoes protected separately, jacket folded flat” say more than “large parcel” and “small parcel.”

Keep a list of the warehouse item references in both scenarios. The goods, quantity, destination and required protection should be the same unless the decision explicitly concerns changing them. If one scenario omits a second jacket altogether, it answers a different question: whether to send that jacket now or later. You can compare that too, but include the eventual second shipment in the cost analysis. An immediate low charge for a smaller package does not automatically mean the whole purchase will cost less to deliver.
Work in consistent units before using any formula

Enter all external dimensions in the units the selected calculator expects. A box measuring 0.4 metres in length is 40 centimetres, and 400 millimetres is the same length again. A typo can move a route outside its size limits by a factor of ten. Confirm that the numbers describe the outer packed carton rather than the product itself or the internal space. Write the units next to every dimension and the actual mass. When sharing measurements with another person, a bare sequence such as “40, 30, 20, 3” is too easy to misread.

Multiply the three external dimensions to obtain the parcel volume, keeping the cubic unit. For example, a hypothetical 42 by 30 by 20 centimetre box occupies 25,200 cubic centimetres. Reducing its height to 16 centimetres gives 20,160 cubic centimetres, a reduction of 5,040 or one fifth of the original volume. This describes space, not money. The route's billing method and rounding determine whether the reduction changes the charge at all. The same difference in volume can matter differently across routes.
Understand which weight the route uses

OrientDig's guide distinguishes estimated billing weight from packed results. It explains that stored goods have a recorded weight with their original packaging and that the system estimates packaging when preparing a parcel. On routes applying volume weight, a volumetric figure can govern when larger than actual weight. Read the current line's conditions for its divisor, unit requirements and other limits. A divisor seen in a forum example or a quote to a different destination cannot establish the terms of your own shipment.

Use a calculation only when its assumptions are explicit. Suppose an illustrative route divided the example box's cubic centimetres by 6,000. The larger arrangement would yield 4.2 kilograms and the smaller 3.36 kilograms before any rounding. If the real parcel weighed 5 kilograms and the hypothetical rule charged the higher value, the physical mass would exceed both dimensional figures. In that example, a one-fifth reduction in volume would not reduce the comparison weight. With a much lighter parcel, the same dimensional change could matter. These figures illustrate the decision, not OrientDig tariffs.
Test the longest side separately from volume

Two boxes can have the same volume and very different shapes. A long narrow box can exceed a route's allowed side length even when its actual mass is low. Calculate or note the longest side in each arrangement. Check any combined-dimension requirements displayed by the route as well. Use the formula specified by the carrier if one appears; length plus girth and a simple sum of dimensions are different expressions. Do not interchange them because both happen to produce a number measured in centimetres.

Imagine comparing a 60 by 20 by 15 centimetre box with a 40 by 30 by 15 centimetre box. Each occupies 18,000 cubic centimetres. If a hypothetical route accepts a maximum side of 50 centimetres, the first shape would fail that single condition and the second would pass it. Passing one rule does not establish complete eligibility, because contents, weight, destination and other size limits may still apply. This is why the three individual sides belong in your saved comparison, not just the computed volume.
Estimate only the variables you cannot yet measure

Early in the buying process, item weights may be seller descriptions or warehouse observations rather than final packed measurements. Keep them labelled. If a rigid item determines the minimum outer length, use that as a constraint on both scenarios. If a soft piece can fold, avoid assuming it can be compressed without affecting its condition. A range with a clear reason is better than an implausibly precise figure. You can update it when the warehouse supplies more information.

Decide whether uncertainty near a threshold is consequential. If both arrangements comfortably fit the route's visible limits and the quoted comparison barely changes, it may not be worth altering valued packaging. If one dimension is close to a listed maximum or a significant charge step, confirm the actual packed measurements before choosing. OrientDig lists rehearsal packing for buyers seeking a packed weight before submission. Ask what additional size information is provided or available for your parcel, and verify the service cost before using it for the comparison.
Recalculate after protection and optional services

External padding, reinforcement and a stronger outer carton may change several inputs at once. A thinner arrangement that requires extra protective spacing may end up nearer the original size than expected. A compact heavy package can cross an actual-weight threshold even when it fits a dimensional limit. Preserve the exact packing instruction used for each quote. A warehouse result for a protected parcel is more informative than a bare product measurement, but only for the goods and protection actually measured.

For a valuable presentation carton, make its preservation an explicit requirement in both candidate arrangements. If the only way to fit a route is to discard it, the comparison becomes a choice between different deliverables. Record that in words rather than presenting the cheaper route as an unqualified improvement. Some buyers value the box; others do not. Your comparison should make the personal trade-off visible and leave the actual carrier rules to the current quote. Avoid authorizing irreversible disposal based solely on an early estimate.
Save a record another person could reproduce

For each scenario, keep its contents, destination, packing description, external dimensions, actual mass, billing basis, currency, quote time and route name. Mark figures that remain estimated. If two quotes differ substantially, isolate the change: did eligibility change, did billing weight change, did a different route become available, or did a service line change? Asking those questions in order makes it easier to spot input mistakes and avoids blaming a price increase on a dimension that never affected the applicable rule.

When you finally choose, retain the result and its reason. “Kept the retail box because the actual mass determined the quote in both measured scenarios” is a reproducible decision. “Split the parcel because the measured longest side exceeded this route's current maximum” is another. At dispatch, check that the recorded outer measurements correspond to the final contents you actually send. Use the result as one reference for a future package, while remembering that a new destination, different item mix or updated carrier conditions can change the conclusion.

A long box can also be easy to misread when a photo is rotated. Identify the longest physical edge before transcribing a photograph, then enter the remaining two edges with their units in the same record.
