Reading OrientDig route exclusions before parcel submission
The cheapest displayed line is useful only if it accepts the actual goods, dimensions and destination. Read restrictions in a deliberate order and keep a record of the case you checked.
Describe the goods as they really are

Start route research with a contents list precise enough for somebody else to assess. “Accessories” might cover textile items, metal fittings, a battery-operated device or a container with liquid. These can raise different carrier questions. Record material, function, quantity and any feature the current service asks about. If you genuinely do not know whether an item contains a particular component, ask the seller or agent before proceeding. A vague category can make an estimate look attractive while leaving the actual eligibility question unanswered.

Keep this record tied to the item or warehouse references. If one parcel contains several different goods, a rule affecting one piece can affect the whole combination. Do not relabel a restricted item as an ordinary garment or omit it to obtain a quote. Ask which service can accept the correctly described contents or whether the shipment needs a different arrangement. The point of reading exclusions early is to avoid paying or packing around a route that cannot handle what you plan to send.
Separate four kinds of restriction

One restriction concerns what a platform or service will handle. Another concerns the selected route's contents or packing conditions. Physical limits concern weight and dimensions, and geographic limits concern destination and delivery area. These categories can overlap, but checking one does not resolve them all. A small parcel that fits the weight limit might still contain an ineligible item. An item eligible in principle may have no available service to your particular address. A general logistics introduction cannot override a condition displayed on the actual route.

When reading a restriction, identify the object it describes. Is the limit per item, per parcel, per side, per shipment value or per destination? If a condition says that a feature requires specific packing, ask whether that packing is available for your order. If a term is unclear, keep the exact wording and route name in your notes and request clarification for the real contents. Avoid turning one buyer's successful shipment into evidence that the written restriction will be ignored for yours.
Compare the dimensions against the exact rule

Use the finished outer box where possible. Write down length, width, height and actual mass with their units. Check which side is longest. Read whether the route states a maximum single side, a sum of dimensions or another formula. A sum of three sides and a length-plus-girth formula are not interchangeable. If final packing is unknown, mark your measurements as estimates and leave a margin for protection. A retail box measured at a maximum length before adding an outer carton deserves particular caution.

For a hypothetical illustration, suppose an item sits in a rigid 48-centimetre retail box and a candidate route lists a 50-centimetre maximum side. Entering 48 gives only two centimetres for outer packaging and protective space across both ends. That may or may not be feasible. Rather than assuming the carton will fit, ask for the outer packed dimension or compare a clearly identified alternative. If discarding the retail box is the only apparent solution, decide whether it is required for protection or presentation before authorizing any change.
Read billing conditions independently of acceptance

OrientDig's weight guide describes actual and volumetric considerations for applicable lines. A parcel can be physically accepted and still be billed on a weight different from its scale reading. Conversely, a calculated dimensional figure below a headline weight limit does not prove the parcel meets every separate size rule. In your comparison, give eligibility and pricing their own columns. Establish acceptance first. Then estimate the amount using the billing basis, unit rules and current charges of the eligible route.

Suppose you have a lightweight but bulky soft item. A route with an attractive rate per kilogram may use volume when it exceeds actual mass. A different line may impose a longest-side condition. Folding the item could make the physical dimensions smaller, but extra protection may partly offset the change. Build two complete scenarios with honest dimensions instead of mixing the lowest weight from one with the smallest box from another. A quote based on a combination you cannot actually ship has little value as a decision tool.
Check destination and delivery service requirements

Use the intended destination and address details that the estimator or route asks for. A route offered to one country, region or type of delivery point may be conditional for another. Check any destination restrictions or special handling notes shown with the result. If delivery timing matters, record whether the displayed interval is described as estimated and when it begins. OrientDig's logistics overview describes multiple stages after warehouse packing, including carrier collection and local delivery. A single date on a shopping plan cannot bypass those stages.

If the route description discusses recipient actions or supporting information, determine what is expected before submitting. For legal or customs questions specific to a destination, use the responsible official authority and current platform or carrier guidance for the actual shipment. An independent spreadsheet cannot determine an individual's legal requirements or guarantee clearance. Keep any relevant communication with the shipment record so that a request received later can be related to the parcel you actually sent.
Check protection and exclusions before interpreting a price difference

A service may accept an object while limiting the circumstances under which loss or damage can be claimed. Acceptance is not the same as comprehensive cover. Read the route's applicable service terms, packing requirements, reporting process and any exclusions relevant to the contents. If an optional protection service appears, identify what is added and what conditions remain. A price difference can reflect different included services, but a higher price alone does not establish more extensive protection.

For a fragile decorative item, ask about the material and how it will be packed instead of asking only whether the line is “safe.” If the rule is ambiguous, a written question naming the item, proposed packing and route can produce an answer you can use. Save that answer and date it. Avoid restating the answer as a general policy for other products or destinations. Conditions can depend on the particular case and may change. The relevant record is the one connected to your actual parcel selection.
Choose a route only after resolving decisive uncertainties

Create a short decision list for each line. Mark each relevant condition as satisfied, unresolved or failed. A failed condition removes that route for the current parcel. An unresolved one tells you exactly what to ask or measure. If a different packing arrangement or split shipment could make a route available, treat that as a new scenario with its own costs and implications for the remaining items. Retain the original so you can see why the change was proposed.

Before payment, check that the selected route, contents and final packed dimensions match the conditions you assessed. If an excluded piece was removed, verify it remains correctly recorded in storage and review its own options. If packaging changed, revisit the physical limits. Save the final route name, quote and reason for selection with the outbound reference. Later, if the service changes or a shipment query arises, you will be able to explain which restrictions you checked, what evidence you used and what the platform confirmed for your particular parcel.

If you are ordering a bundle, check its smallest accessories separately. A listing for a lamp may also show a battery or a power adapter. Ask the seller what actually ships in the selected option, then give that description to the agent before comparing available routes again.
OrientDig help and shipping guidance
OrientDig logistics platform introduction
Following an OrientDig parcel when tracking passes to a local carrier
International tracking can switch providers and use more than one reference. Read the event, location and carrier together to find the last confirmed movement and the right next question.
Identify the outbound shipment before interpreting a scan

Open the OrientDig parcel record associated with the goods you actually submitted for international shipment. Record its reference, selected route and the tracking number shown for that journey. Keep domestic seller tracking elsewhere. A domestic number can show a delivery to the warehouse in China long before your international parcel is packed. Seeing “delivered” against the seller number is therefore not evidence of delivery at your home. First establish which journey, provider and destination each number describes.

Imagine that you bought a backpack and several accessories from two sellers. Their domestic parcels reached the warehouse on separate dates, but you selected the goods for one international package. Your purchase history may now contain two domestic tracking numbers, several warehouse references and one outbound parcel record. If the local delivery company later assigns a replacement number, that is another tracking identity for the outbound journey, not a new shopping order. Make a small map linking the numbers before contacting anyone about a missing update.
Put the displayed event into the delivery sequence

OrientDig's logistics overview describes warehouse packing, collection by a logistics provider, security processing, flight arrangement, possible transit, destination processing, clearance and local delivery. Use that broad sequence as context rather than a promise that every event will appear as a public scan. A shipment may pass through a stage without displaying the exact wording you expect. A service label or account status can also be created before the carrier records physical acceptance of the parcel.

Write the latest confirmed event in plain language. “Carrier received electronic information” usually conveys less than a physical acceptance scan, but read the carrier's actual wording rather than relying on a guessed code translation. “Arrived at sorting facility” describes a facility event and may not establish departure toward the next country. Include the timestamp and location exactly as shown, plus the source of the event. A combined tracking service may summarize several carriers, whereas a provider's own record can clarify which company generated a particular update.
Understand the transition to a delivery partner

An international logistics provider may carry the shipment for one portion and use a destination delivery partner for the final portion. A handoff can involve a different tracking number or the same number recognized by another service. Look for a named local carrier, alternate reference or explicit handoff information in the parcel or carrier record. Where one is supplied, save it beside the original number. If none is supplied, avoid guessing a provider from the format of the digits alone.

A common point of confusion is an alternate number that exists before the local carrier records receiving the parcel. The existence of a local label can identify a planned delivery relationship without proving physical handover. Look for the strongest subsequent observation available, such as a scan recorded by the local provider. If the international record says handed over but the local record shows only electronic information, preserve both statements with their times. This is a useful specific discrepancy to ask about if the expected interval passes.
Compare times, not just the order of lines on screen

Tracking feeds can use local times, different time zones or translated summaries. Check whether a displayed time includes a zone or identifies the facility location. An event posted later on your screen may describe an earlier physical movement. A flight-related status in one country and a facility update in another may appear out of sequence if you compare clock times without their zones. If the time basis is unavailable, mark it unknown and avoid precise claims about how many hours the parcel spent between events.

Keep an event log short and meaningful. For each change that affects your next action, write the date, event, provider and what it actually establishes. You rarely need to copy every repeated transit message. A useful sequence might identify physical acceptance, the last international facility, a named handoff and the first destination-carrier scan. That evidence allows you to ask about a specific gap rather than simply stating that tracking is slow. Avoid sharing a full address or label publicly when discussing a route with other buyers.
Distinguish an estimated interval from a service guarantee

OrientDig notes that the delivery estimate shown after dispatch is indicative and that events such as weather, processing or provider delays can affect progress. Use the estimate displayed for your selected service and the date from which it is measured. It does not necessarily start on the day you paid for the merchandise. Seller fulfillment and domestic delivery precede the international shipment. Count the relevant interval from the appropriate parcel event and check whether the estimate uses business days or calendar days if specified.

An unchanged scan within the displayed estimate can be inconvenient without proving a parcel is lost. Equally, an actionable request for address clarification or collection should not be ignored merely because the estimated end date has not arrived. Read the latest event for an action, deadline or named contact channel. Use the platform and carrier's independently verified services to check the request. Do not send personal information or payment to a contact merely because an unsolicited message repeats a familiar-looking tracking number.
Prepare a useful tracking inquiry

If the status needs clarification, provide the outbound parcel reference, route, original number, verified alternate number and last confirmed event with time and location. State what you expected to see next and which records you checked. “The international provider reports handoff on [date], but the named local provider shows only label information under [reference]” is concise and specific. It gives the platform a concrete relationship to investigate. A screenshot of your entire cart mostly adds unrelated product information.

Where the event says a delivery attempt was made, check the local provider's actual notice before requesting redelivery or collection. Identify the address or pickup instructions privately through the relevant official channel. If the record says delivered but you cannot locate the parcel, check the stated delivery details and any authorized receiving location, then follow the current reporting procedure promptly. Preserve the parcel reference and visible evidence. Do not infer the exact recipient or delivery location solely from a generic “delivered” label.
Close the handoff record at receipt

Once the parcel arrives, match the label or verified local reference to the outbound record. This matters if several packages were travelling at the same time. Compare contents with the selected parcel, not with every purchase on your account. If an item is absent, first establish whether it was supposed to be in this particular shipment. Tracking can support the movement of a parcel; it does not by itself establish what the warehouse packed inside it or the condition of each piece.

Keep the final local number linked to the original until any delivery issue is resolved. If everything arrives as expected, preserve the useful route information for your own future planning, including the time at which the local reference became recognizable. Treat that as an observation from one shipment. It can tell you what records were useful to follow, but it cannot guarantee that a future carrier will use the same partner, publish the same scans or take the same time. The dependable habit is linking the references and reading each event according to the provider that actually recorded it.

When sharing the timeline with a recipient, include the latest confirmed location and the name of the carrier that supplied it. A guess based on the next planned stop may send someone to a local collection point before the parcel has arrived.
OrientDig official help
Writing an OrientDig shopping assistant request for an exact seller option

A usable request lets the purchasing team identify one live offer and one acceptable selection. Prepare the seller link, original option text, unit count and substitution instructions before submitting it.
Decide what information the assistant needs to place this purchase

A shopping assistant cannot reliably infer your preferred version from a picture of a model wearing several pieces. Start with one sentence describing what you intend to buy. It should identify the object, version, size or dimensions, colour and quantity. If an accessory matters, state whether it is included in the selected offer or something you need confirmed. “One navy cropped overshirt in size large, with the detachable collar shown for option B” gives a purchasing assistant a much clearer target than “buy this outfit.”

OrientDig's shopping-assistant guide describes pasting an original seller link or searching for an item and choosing from available results. Use those routes to identify the exact offer first. The stable item identifier and seller information are useful when a short link or translated result is ambiguous. A product page and a shop home page are different kinds of source. If your saved link opens a shop or app promotional screen, recover the individual product page before treating the request as ready for purchase.
Capture the original option wording

Open the live offer and select the version you want. Copy or save the exact option wording alongside any translation. A translation that converts two labels to “dark blue” may hide suffixes distinguishing thickness, cut, season or bundle contents. A single letter, number or short phrase can change what the seller will ship. Record the option code exactly as shown and attach a clear selection screenshot if the available order flow permits. Point out which part of the original wording distinguishes your choice.

Try reopening the link in a separate tab. If it restores the same listing but resets the selected options, the link identifies the product rather than the complete purchase. Keep the option text in the request even when the thumbnail looks right. If the seller's listing has changed since you saved it, use the current live wording and decide whether it still meets your requirements. An old screenshot can explain what you originally wanted. It cannot make an unavailable option orderable or establish a historical price at checkout.
Define the unit and the count

Specify what one unit includes, especially for sets, multipacks and items sold in pairs. Suppose a seller offers a shirt only, shorts only and a two-piece set. Asking for quantity two can mean two complete sets, one top and one bottom, or two copies of the default single garment. State the selected seller option and expected physical contents. For example, “one complete two-piece set, one top and one bottom” is unambiguous if the seller actually offers that choice. Ask first if a desired combination is absent from the listing.

If different colours or sizes are needed, use separate lines in your request. Keep the quantity on each line and add an overall count for your own check. “One navy M and one grey L” lets you compare the confirmation line by line. “Two shirts, navy and grey, M and L” leaves room for the colours and sizes to be paired incorrectly. If the seller has a minimum quantity or different price tiers, ask about the conditions for the exact mix you intend to buy rather than assuming that any combination satisfies the requirement.
State what to do if the exact option is unavailable

A good request distinguishes essential specifications from flexible preferences. Decide in advance whether you accept a different shade, neighbouring size or delayed dispatch. If only the exact version is acceptable, say that the assistant should contact you before purchasing any substitute. If you are open to an alternative, define the condition precisely. “Please show me the brown option if navy is unavailable” asks for information; it does not authorize an automatic switch to brown. Make the difference explicit when the decision matters.

Price changes deserve the same treatment. Preserve the product price shown for the selected option and any domestic delivery line visible at the time of the request. If the order requires your approval for an adjustment, review whether it replaces an amount or adds a new charge. A row with a higher price may represent a different selected variant rather than a seller price increase. Compare seller, option, quantity and included pieces before attributing the change to one cause. Keep any accepted changes with the original request.
Attach only evidence that resolves ambiguity

An annotated image can help identify a particular cuff, badge, pocket or accessory. Explain what it shows and whether it comes from the seller listing, another buyer or your own comparison. A reference from a different seller can illustrate a feature you want, but it cannot prove that your chosen seller offers it. Highlight a specific point rather than attaching a dozen unlabelled pictures. The purchasing assistant should be able to tell which image identifies the option and which merely explains a preference.

For a measurement question, include the chart attached to the exact version and define the endpoints you care about. Ask whether the seller can confirm them before purchase if the information is essential. Some questions are better answered after a physical item reaches the warehouse. OrientDig's detailed-photo guide describes requesting specific angles and measurements on stored items. Decide whether post-purchase inspection is acceptable for your situation. Do not assume that every uncertainty discovered after buying necessarily creates a right to return or exchange the item.
Review the confirmation as a separate document

When the purchase confirmation appears, cover your request and read the confirmation on its own. Does it identify the correct listing, selected model, colour, size, units and quantity? Compare the amount and any domestic delivery or service entries that actually apply. Then uncover your original note and resolve any difference. This check catches errors that a familiar product thumbnail can hide. If the confirmation only says “blue,” verify that the distinguishing version code appears somewhere else before assuming the correct shade and cut were selected.

For a mistake, send one focused correction with the purchase reference and the exact field to change. “Please confirm the cropped navy B version; the confirmation currently displays the long A version” is easier to act on than “the order is wrong.” Check the current order status because the available remedy can change after purchase or seller shipment. If a correction is agreed, save the revised confirmation rather than relying on a chat message alone. The revised record will be your basis for warehouse inspection.
Carry the request forward into a practical warehouse check

When the goods arrive, use the original essential specifications as a short inspection list. For the overshirt, identify the size label, check the cropped shape and verify the detachable collar if it was part of the confirmed option. A full overview can establish the pieces present; a close photograph can establish a particular fastening or label. Tie each observation to the warehouse reference so it remains distinguishable from historical pictures or another item from the same listing.

If the evidence matches, record why the item is ready for the next stage. If it does not, identify the first disagreement between your request, the confirmed purchase and the observed unit. That tells you whether the problem concerns an ambiguous request, a purchase selection error, seller fulfillment or a photograph that simply cannot answer the question. An exact shopping-assistant request thus does more than help someone buy the item. It creates a reference that remains useful through inspection, parcel selection and any later inquiry about what you actually agreed to purchase.
If another buyer is paying for the order, send them the selected option and agreed total in writing before purchase so that they can check the same version.
